newsitem.title: INDIA: India divestment programme falls far short of goal.
newsitem.headline: India divestment programme falls far short of goal.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Saturday the government's ambitious plan to sell about $1.4 billion worth of shares in state-owned firms was unlikely to be achieved by the end of the current fiscal year.
"The present process of disinvestment is nonsensical," Omkar Goswami, professor at New Delhi's Indian Statistical Institute told a conference on divestment of shares in state-owned firms.
The government has set a target of raising 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion) in 1996/97 (April-March) from divestment, or the sale of partial stakes in state-controlled firms.
Last year India raised 3.57 billion rupees ($99.7 million) from divestment, well short of its target of 70 billion ($1.95 billion).
"We cannot hustle the process of disinvestment. Some money will come before March and the rest will come after March," Chidambaram told reporters on the sidelines of the conference.

India had planned to sell a seven percent stake in telecommunications firm Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL) and five percent in crude oil refining company Indian Oil Corp (IOC) in the first round of divestment in 1996/97.
But the government has not yet fixed a date for kicking off the first round of divestment.
"It does not matter as long as the process of disinvestment is credible, transparent and moves along smoothly," Chidambaram said.
The government plans a second tranche after the first round of sell-offs in VSNL and IOC, but time is running out before the 1996/97 year ends on March 31.
Chidambaram said the government's divestment programme should be "enterprise-specific".
The partial privatisations must take into account market conditions, the nature of the sectors in which the firm operate, and the attractiveness of the shares to investors, he said.
Chidambaram said in the past the partial privatisation plan had brought in "little money but a lot of criticism".
The ruling United Front coalition set up a Disinvestment Commission last year to advise the government.
The Commission is not responsible for the first two rounds, but will make recommendations on divestments in 40 state-owned firms in the third phase of the programme.
"The paramount goal of disinvestment is to make the enterprises more efficient, more productive and maximise the return on the capital invested," Chidambaram said.
Goswami said the state-owned units must be first freed "from the tyrannical shackles of the government" and given more freedom to operate to increase their profitability and operational efficiency.
Anthony Browne, a senior official of consultancy group Price Waterhouse, said less government intervention will speed up decision making and improve state firms' performance.
